title: North and South: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Milton and the Machine – First Encounters

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — a close reading of Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage — following Margaret Hale from the Hampshire parsonage to the smoke and clamour of Milton-Northern.
We'll be asking what makes this novel so enduring — its characters, its social vision, its extraordinary prose — and why it still unsettles readers a hundred and seventy years on.
Three guests have agreed to argue with each other — and occasionally with me — about all of it.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong student of the moral imagination in fiction.
He reads novels as tests of character — and he will keep us honest about whether we're reading a story or writing a manifesto.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it cost, in 1850, to be poor in a cotton town.
He will give us the world behind the novel — the institutions, the law, the lived conditions Gaskell drew on.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read North and South as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
She is here for the prose, the feeling, and every line that makes you stop and re-read it.
Today we're beginning where the novel's real argument begins — with Margaret's first encounter with Milton and its people, and what she makes of what she sees.
What strikes me every time I come back to these early chapters is how quickly Gaskell makes Milton feel physical — almost oppressive.
It isn't just that the air is dirty — it's that the air is described as deprived of all revivifying principle.
"deprived of all revivifying principle as it seemed to be here"
That phrase does something remarkable — it gives the industrial air a quality of moral as well as physical exhaustion.
And it's filtered through Margaret's anxiety for her mother — which makes it even more charged.
The domestic and the atmospheric collapse into the same dread.
I think Caroline is right that the atmosphere is powerfully rendered — but I'd resist the temptation to read it as indictment.
What Gaskell is doing in those passages is showing us Milton through Margaret's sensibility — a sensibility formed entirely in the South.
The novel's great project, as I read it, is the education of that sensibility — not its vindication.
And there is already, even here, a seed of self-correction in Margaret.
Consider what she says about Thornton — and notice the candour of it.

"Everything else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so simply—with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother"
She is pronouncing judgement on Thornton and simultaneously revising it — within the same sentence.
That is character developing in real time — and it is the deepest thing the novel does.
Edmund is right that this is Margaret's developing perception — but I think what she perceives is also historically accurate, and that matters.
When Margaret describes the men she sees in the streets of Milton, she is not being melodramatic.
The condition of the handloom weavers, the factory operatives in the late 1840s — the grinding poverty was a matter of parliamentary record.
Listen to what she actually says — this is precise social observation dressed in novelistic language.
"I see men here going about in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only sufferers but haters."
"Not only sufferers but haters" — that is a political diagnosis, and a very acute one.
The resentment of labour that had been dispossessed and degraded — that is the engine of what will eventually become the strike at the centre of this novel.
And the full line carries even more weight when you read the whole passage.
Margaret says this to Thornton directly — she is roused, as Gaskell puts it, to a fond vehemence of defence.
"Now, in the South we have our poor, but there is not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here."
And then — and this is the Gaskell touch I adore — she collapses into a determined silence, angry with herself for having said so much.
She wins the argument and immediately regrets winning it.
That compression — passion, articulation, and then self-rebuke in the space of a paragraph — is simply brilliant characterisation.
James will forgive me if I suggest that the sullen sense of injustice Margaret observes is not quite the same thing as injustice being committed.
She is reading faces in a street — and she is doing so as a stranger, newly arrived, shaped by everything Helstone has made her.
What Gaskell gives us here is not reportage but the phenomenology of displacement — the shock of encountering a world whose values one does not yet understand.
And that, I submit, is the far more interesting subject for a novelist than any social programme.
I don't disagree that Gaskell is a novelist first — but the two things needn't be mutually exclusive.
The phenomenology of displacement, as Edmund puts it, is also a way of making the reader feel what statistics cannot convey.
And there is something else in the domestic passages — the detail about Mrs. Hale's private prayers — that I find quietly devastating.
Margaret steals out of the room having caught only a few words — and those words are a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering.
"a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering"
What Milton costs this family is not abstract — it is paid in the body of one woman, quietly, behind a closed door.
Three very different lenses on the same opening chapters — and already I think we can see the shape of a debate that will carry us through the whole novel.
Is Margaret a reliable moral witness — or a character in the process of being educated out of her prejudices?
And does the novel ultimately vindicate her first impressions, revise them — or, as I suspect, do something rather more complicated than either?
We'll keep those questions alive as we move into the next segment — where we'll be looking at the first full collision between Margaret and Thornton.

segments.title: The Heart of the Matter: Margaret's Moral Education

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We're deep into Elizabeth Gaskell's novel today, and this segment takes us to what I'd call the moral core of the book.
Not the industrial argument, not the romance — though both are present — but the question of how people actually change.
How characters learn, unlearn, and grow — often painfully, often against their own grain.
With me today, as ever, are three readers I trust completely with this material.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral imagination of a man who has spent a lifetime reading great fiction as stories about character tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone gives us the institutional and social world behind Gaskell's scenes — what it actually meant to live inside those structures.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has been reading this novel since she was a teenager, attends to every sentence as if Gaskell wrote it specifically for her — and often seems to have.
Edmund, I want to begin with you — because several of these passages involve figures we might not expect to be the vehicles of moral education.
Mrs. Thornton, Higgins, Thornton himself — all of them teaching and being taught, often without meaning to.
Where do you want to start?
I want to start where Gaskell herself seems to start — with the cost of love that is not returned in kind.
There is a scene in chapter twenty-three that I find almost unbearably moving, and I suspect it is underread.
Mrs. Thornton has just made a rare and almost uncharacteristic appeal to her son — a genuine outpouring.
And he, preoccupied with his own feelings for Margaret, scarcely notices.
Gaskell tells us she crushes down — that is the verb — her personal mortification at the little notice he has taken.
She recovers, she says goodnight, she goes majestically out of the room.
And then Gaskell gives us this:
"But when she got into her own, she locked the door, and sate down to cry unwonted tears."
Unwonted — unused, unfamiliar to herself.
This woman who has armoured herself in pride and will for decades, weeping in a locked room because her son did not notice her love.
That is not social history. That is tragedy.
That word — unwonted — is doing so much work, isn't it.
She is surprised by her own grief. She doesn't know herself in that moment.
And Gaskell has been so precise earlier in the same passage about what Mrs. Thornton suppresses.
She calls it the pang of jealousy that betrayed the intensity of her disregarded love.
"the pang of jealousy that betrayed the intensity of her disregarded love"
Disregarded. Not unrequited — disregarded. It's fiercer than unrequited.
He hasn't withheld his love — he simply hasn't noticed hers enough to have a view about it.
And I think this is Gaskell's most radical insight into mothers and sons.
What strikes me here as a social historian is the grammar of that last gesture.
She went slowly and majestically out of the room — in public, that is her performance.
Then she locks the door. The locked door matters enormously in Victorian domestic space.
Privacy — genuine, physical privacy — was a luxury and a statement.
She is withdrawing into the one space where her social role cannot follow her.
And there, stripped of it, she weeps.
I want to turn from private grief to something more openly combative — and in its way, equally instructive.
There is a superb scene in chapter thirty-eight where Mrs. Thornton pays Margaret a visit that does not go at all as planned.
Margaret sweeps out — and here I relish Gaskell's phrasing — with the noiseless grace of an offended princess.
And Mrs. Thornton is left alone to take stock.
What she thinks is this — and the internal monologue is exquisite:
"My young lady, you've a pretty good temper of your own. You've too much pride and spirit in you for that. I like to see a girl fly out at the notion of being talked about."
She came to remonstrate and ends by admiring.
Not in spite of Margaret's passion — because of it.
That is the moral education of the educators — which Gaskell administers with considerable comic skill.
The comedy there is so precise, isn't it — Mrs. Thornton has quite enough of natural humour to feel the ludicrousness of the position.
She came to shame Margaret, and Margaret has left her standing in an empty room.
There is nothing for it but to show herself out.
And yet — and this is what I love — she isn't angry. She's entertained.
And then comes that devastating aside about Fanny: she'd be giddy, and not bold. She's no courage in her, poor thing.
Mrs. Thornton measures her own daughter against Margaret and finds her wanting — in the very moment she came to reprimand Margaret.
I want to bring in Higgins here, because he is in many ways the most sophisticated moral teacher in the novel — and the least credentialed one.
In chapter twenty-eight, he delivers what is, in effect, a theory of pedagogy — entirely in dialect, entirely from lived experience.
He is speaking about Hamper — a mill owner who tried to correct his workers and failed entirely.
And Higgins explains why, with a metaphor of such precision it would not disgrace a lecture hall.
"Folk who sets up to doctor th' world wi' their truth, mun suit different for different minds; and be a bit tender i' th' way of giving it too, or the poor sick fools may spit it out i' their faces."
Be tender in the way of giving it.
That is a more humane theory of instruction than most official educational doctrine of the 1850s could muster.
And Gaskell gives it to a factory hand, not a reformer or a clergyman.
That passage is one of the great democratic moments in Victorian fiction, and I say that as someone not naturally disposed to democratic readings.
What Higgins articulates is precisely what Burke understood — that legitimate authority depends on the manner of its exercise, not merely its content.
I daresay there's great truth in yon Latin book on your shelves, Higgins says — but it's gibberish and not truth to me unless I know the meaning of the words.
He is not rejecting knowledge. He is making a rigorous epistemological claim about the conditions under which knowledge becomes knowledge.
That is a remarkable thing to put into the mouth of an illiterate mill worker in a mid-Victorian novel.
And now I want to bring in the passage I find most startling in terms of Margaret's own voice — chapter thirty-seven, where she tries to dissuade Higgins from going south.
Because this is Margaret as teacher — and she is brilliant, and she is passionate, and she is also somewhat frightening.
She conjures the agricultural south with an almost Dantean intensity.
Listen to this:

"Those that have lived there all their lives, are used to soaking in the stagnant waters. They labour on from day to day, in the great solitude of steaming fields — never speaking or lifting up their poor, bent, downcast heads."
Poor, bent, downcast heads. I have to stop there every time.
Three adjectives, perfectly weighted — physical, moral, and spiritual collapse all at once.
And she tells him: it would eat you away like rust. You of all men are not one to bear a life among such labourers.
She knows him. That is Margaret's education working — she has truly learned to see him.
That passage is also, I have to say, one of the most accurate accounts of agricultural labour in Victorian fiction.
The hard spadework robs their brain of life — Gaskell is describing something that contemporary observers of rural poverty were documenting in parliamentary reports.
The isolation, the repetition, the cognitive dimming — these were features of agricultural piece-work that kept labourers in a state of near-total intellectual deprivation.
And Margaret has absorbed this, not from reports, but from direct observation during her years in Helstone.
The south she defends earlier in the novel is not the south she describes here. She has changed her testimony.
I want to bring Thornton into this now — because his moral education, I would argue, is the most practically expressed in the novel.
In chapter forty-two, he describes the origins of a communal dining scheme for his workers — and the telling of it is rather wonderful.
He happened to call on Higgins one day and saw, as he puts it:
"such a miserable black frizzle of a dinner — a greasy cinder of meat"
That detail lodged in him. He thought about it. He devised a scheme.
Then Higgins independently proposed the same scheme — and Thornton confesses he was, as he says, a little riled.
He thought of throwing the whole thing overboard — his own words — simply because he would not receive the credit.
But he did not. He took the part assigned to him — something like that of a steward to a club.
For a man of Thornton's pride, that is a very considerable act of moral discipline — and Gaskell lets him narrate it with deliberate understatement.
The phrase that stays with me is his friend — or his enemy — the man I told you of.
That little self-correction — or his enemy — is doing so much emotional work.
He cannot quite yet name what Higgins is to him. The category hasn't formed.
And I think that uncertainty — held in that single parenthetical — is where Gaskell shows us character in the act of changing.
What is also striking, institutionally, is what this scheme represents.
Cooperative provisioning — bulk buying and communal cooking — was an actual working-class strategy of the period, pioneered not by employers but by the workers themselves.
The Rochdale Pioneers had formalised this just a decade before Gaskell was writing.
So when Thornton becomes a steward to his workers' scheme, he is not merely swallowing his pride — he is stepping into an already existing tradition of working-class self-help.
And Gaskell knew this. The novel is not naive about who invented what.
I want to close my contribution to this segment with the passage that I find most quietly devastating in the whole sequence.
Chapter forty-six. Margaret is with Mr. Bell, who is in good spirits.
And she is not. Her thoughts are entirely elsewhere.
She has concluded — as a conviction now, not merely a fear — that Thornton no longer holds his former good opinion of her.
And she is careful, even in her own interior, to distinguish what she wants from what she has resolved not to want.
She has resolved never to dwell on his love. She keeps rigidly to that resolution.
What she cannot bear to lose is something more precise — and Gaskell finds the exact words for it:
"the respect and high regard which she had hoped would have ever made him willing, in the spirit of Gerald Griffin's beautiful lines, to turn and look back when thou hearest the sound of my name."
To turn and look back when thou hearest the sound of my name.
Not love. Not possession. Simply — to be remembered with honour by someone whose honour you have desired.
I find that passage almost unbearable to read aloud.
Because what Margaret has done is perform an exquisite act of self-discipline — she has walled off the larger hope.
And then discovered that what remains, even when you wall it off, is still painful enough to undo her.
The modesty of the wish makes it more heartbreaking, not less.
And yet she is wrong, of course — Thornton has not ceased to regard her. But she cannot know that.
That gap — between what a person believes about how they are seen, and how they are actually seen — is one of the novel's great structural ironies.
And Gaskell maintains it with remarkable discipline right to the end.

What this segment has brought into focus for me is how much of the moral education in this novel happens sideways — through observation, through accident, through the person you came to correct teaching you something instead.
Mrs. Thornton locked in her room. Thornton swallowing his pride over a dining scheme. Margaret telling Higgins what the south really is — and in doing so, revealing how far she has come from it.
These are not dramatic conversions. They are the slow, resistant, often painful adjustments of people who are genuinely trying to be better.
We'll take a short break, and when we return, we'll be looking at what the novel asks of us as readers — what it expects us to have learned by the time it ends.
Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the podcast that takes Elizabeth Gaskell's industrial masterpiece apart, scene by scene, to see what makes it endure.
I'm your host, and joining me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that literature lives or dies on moral imagination — not social programme.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the hard facts — what poverty actually meant, how industrial law actually worked.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager, and who notices things in the prose that most readers walk straight past.
Today's segment is Capital and Conscience: Thornton's Crisis.
We're looking at the full arc — from the grinding poverty of the Higgins household to Margaret's extraordinary offer to save Thornton's mill.
James, you've been given the passages that cut closest to the social bone — let's start with you.
Thank you. What strikes me first about these passages is the extraordinary precision of Gaskell's social observation — she never lets you forget what poverty looks and sounds like.
When Margaret visits the Higgins household and finds Nicholas away, Gaskell gives us this portrait of the younger sister:
"A great slatternly girl, not so old as Bessy, but taller and stronger, was busy at the wash-tub, knocking about the furniture in a rough capable way."
That phrase — rough capable — is doing enormous work. It is not condemnation. It is not sentimentality. It is simply the fact of a girl doing what must be done.
Gaskell understands that the poor are not picturesque. They are exhausted, noisy, making do.
And Margaret — this is important — doesn't flinch. She unlooses Bessy's bonnet strings. She acts.
That detail of the bonnet strings — I've thought about it across multiple readings. It is such a small gesture. And it is everything.
Gaskell doesn't have Margaret deliver a speech. She has her loosen the strings so Bessy can breathe.
And then Nicholas comes home and delivers one of the most quietly devastating lines in the whole novel.
"I could wish there were a God, if it were only to ask Him to bless thee."
The conditional tense. I could wish. He doesn't believe. But he reaches for something beyond himself because this woman has been kind to his daughter.
That is Gaskell at the very top of her powers.
I would resist the impulse to read that passage primarily as a social document, as instructive as it is in that regard.
What Gaskell has constructed there is a scene about the reach of goodness across difference — not class difference alone, but metaphysical difference.
Nicholas Higgins does not believe in God. And yet the one thing he desires at that moment is a God to whom he might express gratitude.
That is not politics. That is moral imagination of the highest order — the imagination of a novelist who can hold contradiction without resolving it.
That contradiction has a material dimension too, Edmund, which I don't think we should separate out quite so cleanly.
Higgins lives in a world where the Church has largely failed the working poor. His scepticism is not abstract.
And Bessy's death, when it comes, is reported to Margaret with a kind of folk poetry that breaks the heart. Mary tells her:
"She were never tired o' talking o' yo'. She used to say yo' were the prettiest thing she ever clapped eyes on. She loved yo' dearly."
And then — and this is what stops me every time — the last words: 'Keep father fro' drink.'
A dying girl's final thought is not for herself. It is for her father and for the woman who was kind to her.
That is the burden the working poor carried — love and vigilance without respite, even at the last.
The dialect in that passage is so carefully rendered. 'Clapped eyes on.' 'Father fro' drink.' Gaskell had clearly listened.
She doesn't smooth it into standard English to make it easier for her drawing-room readership. She leaves it in its own register.
That, to me, is an act of literary respect. These people's voices deserve to be heard as they actually spoke.
I want to bring in the Thornton household now, because Gaskell is doing something equally fine in a very different register.
The portrait of Mrs. Thornton's feeling for her son is one of the subtler achievements of the novel. The narrator draws the distinction with great delicacy:

"She never called her son by any name but John; 'love,' and 'dear,' and such like terms, were reserved for Fanny. But her heart gave thanks for him day and night; and she walked proudly among women for his sake."
The tenderness she withholds from John is itself the mark of her deepest feeling for him. The 'but' in that sentence is doing all the work.
It is a Johnsonian insight: that the truest affections are not always the most demonstrative.
That passage also illuminates the class dynamics at the heart of the novel. Mrs. Thornton is a self-made woman in the sense that her identity is entirely built on her son's success.
And Fanny, who has inherited the comfort without the struggle, is — in her mother's private assessment — simply inadequate.
The narrator tells us that Mrs. Thornton felt 'an unconscious contempt for a weak character.' That is a remarkably frank judgement by a mother about her own child.
It tells us something about what the industrial north demanded of its people: that weakness, in this world, is not merely inconvenient but almost morally disqualifying.
And then that ethos collides violently with its own contradictions when we come to Thornton and Higgins's confrontation over work in Chapter 38.
James, you have that passage too — it's quite an extraordinary scene.
Extraordinary, and extraordinarily uncomfortable. Higgins has swallowed his pride and come to Thornton asking for work — not for himself, but to support another man's children.
And Thornton refuses him, on grounds that are — and this is what makes the scene so morally complex — actually coherent.
He says to Higgins:

"You'd be taking less wages than the other labourers — all for the sake of another man's children. Think how you'd abuse any poor fellow who was willing to take what he could get to keep his own children. You and your Union would soon be down upon him."
He's calling Higgins a scab by his own union's standards. It is a brutal, precise, entirely accurate accusation.
What Gaskell is showing us is that the systems of solidarity the workers have built can themselves become instruments of exclusion.
Thornton is not wrong. That is the discomfiting thing. His logic is impeccable, and he knows it, and he deploys it to refuse a man work.
This is where Gaskell's moral intelligence is most demanding. She will not give us a simple villain. She gives us a man of principle, acting on principle, producing an unjust result.
That is the proper province of the novel — to present dilemmas that no political tract can resolve.
And notice how Thornton refuses to leave cleanly. He says, 'Let me pass' — and then he keeps talking. He cannot quite walk away.
He repeats 'I'll not give you work' twice. The repetition is a tell. He is convincing himself as much as he is refusing Higgins.
Gaskell is extraordinary at this — at showing us the gap between what a character says and what they feel in the same breath.
Which brings us to the culmination of all these threads — Margaret's offer in Chapter 52.
This is the scene where the capital and the conscience finally meet, face to face. Caroline, I know you have strong feelings about this moment.
Strong feelings — that is one way to put it. This scene moves me every single time, and I have read it more times than I can count.
Margaret is trembling. She is fumbling through papers. She is in a state of barely controlled agitation, and she is trying desperately to present it all as mere business.
Gaskell captures the exact quality of that performance. She goes on, the narrator tells us, 'rapidly turning over some law papers... in a trembling hurried manner.'
And then the proposal itself — I want to read it because the arithmetic matters, the specificity is everything:

"if you would take some money of mine, eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds, lying just at this moment unused in the bank, and bringing me in only two and a half per cent. — you could pay me much better interest, and might go on working Marlborough Mills."
Eighteen hundred and fifty-seven pounds. Not a round number. A real sum. The kind of figure that only someone who actually has the money — and has looked at the account — would name.
Gaskell makes Margaret's generosity utterly concrete. It is not an impulse. It is a decision.
What is remarkable is that Margaret insists on framing this as advantageous to herself. She is 'most anxious to have it all looked upon in the light of a mere business arrangement.'
That is pride of a very particular kind — not cold pride, but the pride that refuses to allow its own generosity to humiliate the recipient.
Burke would have recognised it: the instinct to clothe charity in the forms of dignity, so that both parties may survive the transaction with honour.
There is also something quietly revolutionary in that scene from an economic standpoint. A woman of independent means offering capital to a male industrialist on her own terms.
In 1855, when this was published, a married woman could not have done this. Margaret is unmarried, she has inherited, and she acts.
The novel is acutely aware of that legal fact. Margaret's independence is not incidental — it is structural to what she is able to offer.
And then Thornton speaks her name. That is all the narrator tells us at the end of that passage — just that his voice was 'hoarse, and trembling with tender passion.'
Gaskell cuts away at that moment. She doesn't give us the words. The scene arrests itself at the very instant before everything changes.
That is the technique of a writer who understands that silence can carry more than any sentence she might write.
We've moved from a dying girl's last wish to a trembling industrialist hearing his name spoken in an empty room — and Gaskell has connected every thread.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you. We'll return shortly to look at how the novel imagines what comes after the crisis: the question of what Thornton and Margaret might actually build together.

segments.title: Close Reading: The Strike Scene and Its Reverberations

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of North and South Unpacked, where we slow down and read closely.
Today we're focusing on the human relationships that grow out of the industrial landscape — and what those relationships reveal about class, kindness, and belonging.
With me are Sir Edmund Leigh, whose moral imagination brings a particular clarity to characters under pressure.
Professor James Blackstone, who keeps us honest about what it actually meant to be a workman in mid-Victorian Milton.
And Caroline Woodcourt, whose ear for the verbal music of this novel is, quite simply, unmatched.
Let's begin with the moment Margaret first truly sees Nicholas Higgins — not as a type, but as a person.
What strikes me every time I return to this passage is how economical Gaskell is with the moment of recognition.
There's no grand introduction, no dramatic scene of suffering thrust in Margaret's face.
Just a careworn man on a Milton street who says something unexpectedly kind.
Gaskell sets it up beautifully — several men have already catcalled Margaret that same day.
And then this one man says something entirely different:
"You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face."
There's warmth there, but also something elegiac — he's admiring her youth while implying he has little left to smile about himself.
And Margaret receives it that way — she smiles back, and a silent recognition is born.
Caroline is quite right to dwell on the silence.
Gaskell tells us they have never exchanged a word beyond that first compliment — and yet this man holds more interest for Margaret than anyone else in Milton.
That is not a social observation — it is a moral one.
Margaret responds to character — to the quality of a soul visible in a single glance — rather than to station or circumstance.
Burke would have recognised this — genuine sympathy, he argued, is not the province of any class.
It is the province of good people.
I take Edmund's point about individual goodness, but I'd press on the context a little.
This is a man described as poorly-dressed, careworn, and walking with a daughter who is, as Gaskell puts it, still more unhealthy than he was himself.
These are the specific physical marks of the cotton trade — long hours, dust in the lungs, wages that cannot sustain health.
Gaskell doesn't labour the point — she never does — but the details are precise and she knew exactly what they meant.
The kindness of that careworn man is more striking, not less, when you understand what his daily life actually was.
And then Gaskell takes this fragile connection one step further — with something as simple as a handful of spring flowers.
This is one of those moments I return to whenever I want to remember why I love this novel.
Margaret has been out in the fields beyond Milton — early spring, picking hedge and ditch flowers.
Gaskell names them — dog-violets, lesser celandines — and she adds, with beautiful restraint, "an unspoken lament in her heart for the sweet profusion of the South."
That phrase, "sweet profusion" — it does so much work.
It's everything Helstone was: abundance, ease, beauty given freely by the earth.
And then she meets the girl, who looks wistfully at the flowers — and Margaret simply gives them to her, on impulse.
No speech, no deliberation — it's a gesture that bypasses everything social and just connects, human to human.
That spontaneity is essential to what Gaskell is showing us about Margaret's character.
She acts before social calculation can intervene.
And notice — Margaret's mother is not present on this walk.
Her father has gone into Milton on business — Margaret is, for this moment, entirely free of the drawing-room's invisible rules.
Which brings me to the scene at home, when Mrs. Hale's drawing-room rules reassert themselves with considerable force.
Ah yes — the conversation about trade, and whether Mr. Thornton can be considered a gentleman.
I confess this passage always makes me rather impatient with Mrs. Hale.
But what I find historically interesting is Margaret's counter-argument — because she's not dismissing class, she's redefining it.
She says, with admirable directness:
"I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes."
That's a genuinely radical idea in 1855 — that ladyhood is a property of character, not of exemption from labour.
And she extends it to Thornton — he can't help being in trade, poor fellow, because his education didn't fit him for anything else.
It's affectionate, and slightly patronising, and it suggests she's working something out about him in real time.
The "poor fellow" is doing a great deal of work, isn't it.
She defends him to her mother — and then immediately retreats to her room because she cannot bear much more.
Gaskell puts that detail in so quietly: "just now she could not bear much more."
Margaret is tired, and brave, and keeping so much inside — and that sentence lands like a hand on the shoulder.
What I find remarkable across all these passages is the transformation they chart — not of society, but of a person's inner world.
After the encounter with Higgins and his daughter, Margaret walks home — and Gaskell shows us precisely what has shifted.
"From that day Milton became a brighter place to her.
It was that in it she had found a human interest."
Not the seasons, not the passage of time — a human interest.
Gaskell understood — as Johnson did — that it is persons, not places, that make life endurable.
And that human interest is tested, and proved, all the way to the end of the novel.
There's a moment late in the book — after everything, after the strike, after Thornton's mill has failed — that I find extraordinarily moving.
Thornton tells Margaret that his former workers have petitioned him — asking to work for him again if he ever can employ men.
"I had a round-robin from some of my men — I suspect in Higgins' handwriting — stating their wish to work for me, if ever I was in a position to employ men again on my own behalf."
Higgins, who led the strike against Thornton, is likely the man who wrote the petition asking him back.
That is what sustained human interest actually produces — not sentiment, but loyalty grounded in mutual respect.
And Thornton's response to it — "That was good, wasn't it?" — is so disarming.
This is a man who has lost his mill, and what moves him is that his workers still want him.
He asks Margaret if it's good — almost like a child needing confirmation — and it tells you everything about how far he has come.
That's the arc: from the man who wouldn't unbend to his workers, to the man who is moved to tears that they haven't forgotten him.
From a silent recognition on a Milton street to a round-robin in Higgins' handwriting — the novel has traced something remarkable.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you.
We'll return shortly to look more closely at how Gaskell handles power — and the limits of what kindness alone can do.

segments.title: Laughter, Irony, and the Lighter Thread

utterances.text: Welcome to this part of our conversation, where we take a step back from the novel's grander architectural concerns and ask: what makes North and South funny?
Because it is funny — often, quietly, and with tremendous precision.

To explore that lighter thread, I'm especially glad to have Caroline Woodcourt with us — a critic who has been re-reading this novel since her teens and who notices what the rest of us miss on a first pass.
Edmund Leigh is here too, ready, I suspect, to remind us that comedy in a novel is never merely decoration.
And James Blackstone brings his historian's eye for what these social comedies actually cost the people inside them.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because there's a moment in Chapter Seven that I think encapsulates something very Gaskellian about social comedy.
Yes, and it's a moment that goes off so quietly you can miss it entirely on a first reading.
Thornton has called at the Hales' house — twice, we're told — and Margaret has to receive him alone, which is awkward enough.
But what Gaskell gives us is this extraordinary little display of composed social management from Margaret.
She identifies him — 'Mr. Thornton, I believe!' — at precisely the moment when, we're told, his own words simply would not come.
"Mr. Thornton, I believe!"
That exclamation mark is doing so much work — it's gracious, it's definitive, and it ever so gently rescues the situation from his embarrassment.
And then she immediately gives him a narrative — father was here, father has gone, father will be back — all without missing a beat.
The comedy is in the perfection of it, and in the fact that Thornton is, for once, completely outmanoeuvred.
What strikes me about that scene is that Gaskell is perfectly aware she has written a comedy of manners, and she plays it with a straight face throughout.
The humour is never telegraphed — there is no wink to the reader.
Which is precisely what makes it so enjoyable.
And the comedy deepens considerably when we move to Chapter Nine and hear Thornton's account of that same encounter — from his own thoroughly wounded perspective.
He confesses to his mother — with what Gaskell calls 'a short scornful laugh' — that Margaret treated him with, and I do relish this phrase —
"a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it."
'A strong flavour of contempt' — that is the phrasing of a man who has been stung and who is still, rather magnificently, feeling it.
There is genuine comedy in the precision of his injury.
And then he goes even further — which is where Gaskell really lets herself go.
The image he reaches for is magnificent in its self-pity.
"She held herself aloof from me as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal."
'Unwashed.' That word is doing extraordinary work.
He could have said 'humble vassal' and left it there — but 'unwashed' tells us exactly how diminished he felt, how class-conscious the encounter was for him.
And the comedy is that this enormously proud, self-made man has allowed a girl he met once to reduce him to a medieval serf in his own private imagination.
There is something historically quite pointed in that 'unwashed,' though — and Gaskell, I think, knows exactly what she's doing with it.
The phrase 'the great unwashed' was already in common currency — it referred, with a certain casual contempt, to the labouring classes.

Thornton is a manufacturer — he employs those people, he comes from that world, and a southern clergyman's daughter has somehow managed to make him feel that he belongs among them rather than above them.
The comedy has a very sharp edge when you put it in that context.
And yet Gaskell's comedy is never simply at Thornton's expense — she's too fond of him for that.
Caroline, there's a scene in Chapter Twenty — the dinner party — where the comedy of observation becomes something closer to tenderness.
Oh, that scene is one of my absolute favourites in the whole novel.

Thornton arrives, he's carrying the weight of the strike — his mill is in crisis — and Gaskell gives us this extraordinarily delicate portrait of a man trying very hard to be present while being pulled entirely elsewhere.
And then — he looks at Margaret.
And the way Gaskell renders what he sees — in that long, almost painterly passage — is both satirically precise and completely besotted.
He's watching her talk to his sister Fanny, and the contrast Gaskell draws is beautifully unkind to poor Fanny.
"he saw his sister's restless way of continually arranging some part of her gown, her wandering eyes, now glancing here, now there, but without any purpose in her observation"
That is a portrait of a woman with nothing interesting going on in her mind — and it is completely devastating.

And then the same sentence pivots immediately to Margaret's eyes — 'the large soft eyes that looked forth steadily at one object' — and the whole thing becomes an act of worship dressed up as observation.
The comedy there is entirely at Thornton's expense, and he can do nothing about it — because he's the one who is looking.
What I find particularly fine is the last stroke Gaskell delivers: 'Mr. Thornton sighed as he took in all this with one of his sudden comprehensive glances.'
He sighed.
This is a man of iron will, master of a great mill, engaged in a bitter industrial dispute — and he sighs because a young woman is beautiful.
Gaskell's sense of humour is in full possession of that sentence, and I think she relishes it.
And then — and this is the moral precision beneath the comedy — he turns his back on her, and throws himself with all his heart and soul into a conversation with Mr. Hale.
He disciplines himself.
I want to move us somewhere quite different before we leave this topic, because there's a passage assigned here that I think complicates the idea of Gaskell's 'lighter thread' considerably.
Higgins's speech to Mr. Hale in Chapter Twenty-Eight is often read as polemical, which it is — but it has a very dark comedy running through it.
He's dismantling Hale's religious consolations with the bluntness of a man who has simply never been able to afford them.
And the line he arrives at is one of the great comic-tragic formulations in Victorian fiction, I'd argue.
"The purse and the gold and the notes is real things; things as can be felt and touched; them's realities; and eternal life is all a talk."
There is a grim wit in that — 'them's realities' — the grammar itself enacting the directness, the physicality of his worldview.
And then he catches himself — remembers Mr. Hale is a parson out of work — and offers the most economical courtesy in the novel: he won't speak disrespectfully of a man in the same fix as himself.
That correction — 'I ax your pardon, sir; yo'r a parson out o' work, I believe' — is so perfectly timed.

He's been building to this devastating dismissal of religion, and then the brake goes on — not because he's wrong, in his own terms, but because he's a decent man who notices the human being in front of him.
Gaskell gives Higgins a moral quickness that her more conventionally educated characters often lack.
And that instinct — that quick, unschooled grace — is itself a form of humour, because it arrives completely unexpectedly.

Higgins is, in certain respects, the novel's most morally complete character — and the comedy of his scenes arises from the fact that he knows it and doesn't particularly care whether anyone else knows it.

There is a self-possession in his voice — even across the dialect — that reminds one of Johnson's remark that every man thinks meanly of himself for not having been a soldier, or not having been at sea.
Higgins has been at sea, in the truest sense, and he speaks with that authority.

What strikes me, having heard all of this, is how consistently Gaskell's comedy is a comedy of clarity — of people seeing and saying exactly what they mean, at the moment when convention demands they do not.
Margaret naming Thornton before he can name himself.
Thornton discovering, to his horror, the exact word for how small Margaret made him feel.
Higgins cutting through an entire theology with three words: 'them's realities.'
In our next section, we'll ask how that same clarity operates when the stakes are at their highest — in the novel's great scenes of conflict and confrontation.

segments.title: The North and South Divide: Narrative Technique and Social Truth

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked, the podcast that takes Elizabeth Gaskell's great novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we begin with the novel's sharpest preoccupations: the divide between North and South, the way Gaskell uses narrative technique to illuminate social truth.
With me today are three brilliant readers of this novel, each bringing a distinct lens.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is, above all, a moral imagination at work — not a social programme dressed in plot.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in law and in life, to be poor in an industrial town in the eighteen-fifties.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it more times than she can count — and whose ear for Gaskell's prose is, quite simply, the best I know.
Let's begin at the very beginning — or near enough — with Margaret Hale arriving, as a child of nine, into the London world that will shape her.
What strikes me first about that nursery scene is how deeply Gaskell understands the violence of displacement — and how quietly she renders it.
Margaret is brought, Gaskell tells us, 'all untamed from the forest' — a phrase that carries the whole weight of the South's pastoral mythology.
But consider what Gaskell does with the architecture of that house.
The child imagines her father and aunt as being either up in the sky or — and I find this quite extraordinary —
'deep down in the bowels of the earth.'
That is not domestic realism — that is gothic geometry, the spatial imagination of a frightened child rendered with perfect precision.
And all of this, one must note, is achieved through free indirect style — we are inside Margaret's childhood memory, inside the adult Margaret's remembering, simultaneously.
Edmund, yes — and what undoes me every time I read that passage is the suppression.
The little girl cries bitterly — but then hushes herself, not because she is comforted, but because her father might be made unhappy.
At nine years old, she is already performing composure for someone else's sake.
And Gaskell makes it worse — she adds that the child thought it was wrong even to feel grief at all.
The whole arc of Margaret's character — the famous haughtiness, the cool bearing — it all roots here, in a nine-year-old who learned that her feelings were an imposition.
Gaskell's narrative technique at its finest: no explanation, no authorial intrusion — just the fact, and you draw the line yourself.
I want to hold onto that phrase 'her grander circumstances' for a moment, because it does real social work in that passage.
The Hales are a country parsonage family — respectable, educated, but not wealthy.
Mrs. Shaw's Harley Street household represents a different register of gentility entirely — one predicated on money, on servants, on the careful management of appearance.
And Gaskell captures this through the nurse — not through a lecture on class, but through 'clean hands and torn frocks.'
'She remembered the dark, dim look of the London nursery, presided over by an austere and ceremonious nurse, who was terribly particular about clean hands and torn frocks.'
That nurse is the disciplinary instrument of a social class — she enforces its codes on children's bodies before they are old enough to resist.
Gaskell knows this, and she trusts us to know it too.
And that Margaret — the girl who learned to suppress her grief, to perform composure — is the same Margaret who walks into Thornton's Milton and is immediately read as haughty.
Which brings us to one of the most remarkable pieces of double-vision in the novel — the scene where Thornton first really looks at her, and misreads everything he sees.
This passage is where Gaskell's narrative technique becomes almost unbearably sophisticated.
We are given Margaret's interiority — she is tired, she would rather be silent, she is simply being courteous because she feels she owes it to herself.
And then Gaskell pivots — without warning — into Thornton's perception of her.
And what he sees is this —

'her round white flexile throat rising out of the full, yet lithe figure; her lips moving so slightly as she spoke, not breaking the cold serene look of her face with any variation from the one lovely haughty curve.'
'Flexile' — that word alone is worth a week's thought.
It suggests suppleness, yielding — the very opposite of the rigidity Thornton is projecting onto her.
Caroline has put her finger on something essential — and I would press it further.
What Gaskell is doing here is not merely ironic — it is tragic.
Thornton interprets Margaret's exhaustion and courtesy as contempt and pride.
And Gaskell gives us — with that ruthless omniscience — his actual thought: he 'almost said to himself that he did not like her.'
'Almost' — because, of course, he cannot quite commit to it.
The man is already caught, and he doesn't know it yet.
The novel's entire moral architecture — the slow, painful education of two proud people — is encoded in that single 'almost.'
There's a class dimension here that I think we mustn't let slide past.
Thornton is not simply a proud man misreading a proud woman.
He is a self-made manufacturer — Gaskell is quite precise about this — who has clawed his way out of poverty and knows the codes of the southern gentry only as an outsider looking in.
Margaret, for all her impecunious parsonage background, carries those codes in her body — in the very bearing that Gaskell describes.
And then there's the small, devastating detail: Thornton is described as 'not over-brushed, nor over-polished' after his rough encounter with Milton's streets.
The gentleman versus the manufacturer — it's there in the dust on his coat, before a word is spoken about class.
And into this charged space steps a third perspective — not Margaret's, not Thornton's, but his mother's.
Mrs. Thornton's voice is one of the most extraordinary things in the novel — passionate, partisan, and in its own way, completely honest.
Mrs. Thornton is the character I find most interesting precisely because she is the least literary, the least polished — and the most completely true.
She does not argue her case — she erupts it.
Gaskell gives us the inside of her head as a kind of furious catechism —
'Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind.'
That last clause — 'I can see what's what, and not be blind' — is almost juridical.
She is offering evidence, not sentiment — presenting her son's character as a matter of established fact, against which Margaret's disdain is simply an error.
And yet she is also wrong — magnificently, understandably wrong — about what Margaret actually feels.
That is Gaskell's great ironic gift in this novel: every character's passion is entirely intelligible from within, and entirely limited from without.
Mrs. Thornton ends with 'I hate her' — three words that are the whole novel's central tension expressed at its most naked.
Burke would have recognised the type — the matriarch whose pride is her love, and whose love is a form of territorial defence.
What I love about that passage is the comic ferocity of it — but also the pathos underneath.
Mrs. Thornton knows what Fanny is — she says so plainly — and the contrast with John is everything to her.
This woman has built her entire emotional life around one person's worth, and she is now watching that worth go unrecognised.
The violence of 'I hate her' is the violence of someone who has nowhere else to put the pain.
And we find the most searching assessment of Margaret's worth — and what it demands of those who love her — in a passage that arrives much later in the novel.
Mr. Bell's rebuke to Thornton, for describing Margaret as merely a 'beautiful creature,' is one of the passages I return to whenever I need to remember what this novel is actually about.
This is, I think, the most morally concentrated passage in the novel — and it is given to the most unexpected speaker.
Mr. Bell is not, in the ordinary sense, a romantic figure.
Yet here he articulates something that cuts to the heart of what love — serious love — is supposed to do to a person.
He says —
'to have loved her without return would have lifted you higher than all those, be they who they may, that have ever known her to love.'
Not reciprocal love — unrequited love — as a moral elevation.
That is not a Victorian commonplace — that is a genuinely radical ethical claim, and Gaskell puts it in the mouth of a minor character, almost casually.
The line that stops me every time is the ending of that speech: 'Do you speak of her as you would of a horse or a dog?'
'Do you speak of her as you would of a horse or a dog?'
It lands like a slap — and it's funny, in the blackest possible way.
But it also tells us exactly what Mr. Bell thinks Thornton has reduced Margaret to — a possession to be appraised, not a soul to be honoured.
And behind it is the same Gaskell who showed us Margaret's childhood tears being hushed in the dark — always watching for the moment when a human being is not seen as fully human.
Edmund speaks of this as a radical ethical claim, and I think he's right — but I'd add that it's also a social claim.
Thornton describing Margaret as merely a 'beautiful creature' is the language of a man who has spent his life pricing things — labour, cotton, machinery.
He has not yet learned to see people — including his own workers — as something other than quantifiable assets.
Bell's rebuke isn't just about Margaret — it's about what kind of man Thornton is, and what he still needs to become.
That is the novel's entire educational arc in miniature — and Gaskell lets a secondary character deliver it with devastating economy.
Three passages, three registers — the gothic tenderness of childhood memory, the tragic irony of misperception, and the moral bracing of Mr. Bell's rebuke.
And in each of them, Gaskell's narrative technique is doing something that simple social polemic could never do — it is making us inhabit the misunderstanding from the inside.
We'll be back in a moment — and when we return, we'll be going deeper into the industrial world of Milton, and what Gaskell understood about the relationship between masters and men.

segments.title: Closing: Transformation Complete – Love, Class, and Belonging

utterances.text: We've travelled a long way in this episode — from Milton's smoke-filled streets to the drawing rooms of Helstone, from strikes and standoffs to something altogether more private.
And we arrive, finally, at one of the novel's most quietly extraordinary sequences: Margaret Hale, pouring tea, and John Thornton, watching.
It sounds domestic, even trivial — and yet Gaskell makes it one of the most electrically charged scenes in Victorian fiction.
Caroline, I want to start with you — you've called this passage one you return to again and again.
Every single time.
Because Gaskell does something here that is almost novelistically dangerous — she gives us the entire interior of a man falling in love, through a bracelet.
A bracelet sliding down a wrist, over and over, while he is supposed to be listening to her father talk.
The narrator tells us, with perfect deadpan composure, that it seemed to fascinate him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh — and then to mark the loosening, the fall.
He could almost have exclaimed — 'There it goes again!'
That exclamation mark is doing so much work — all that bottled intensity, comic and yearning at once.
Gaskell lets us laugh at him — and then catches us feeling something tender for him in the same breath.
And what is so beautifully managed is that Margaret is entirely unaware of his attention — or at least chooses to appear so.
She is enduring a headache, fulfilling her duty, resolved — as the narrator puts it — to throw herself into the breach rather than let her father's guest feel neglected.
There is something Johnsonian about that — the insistence on doing the decent thing even when one would rather lie down in a darkened room.
And then the passage gives us this extraordinary vignette of Mr. Hale taking her little finger and thumb in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues.

She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues.
The proud air of an unwilling slave — and yet that eye catching the moment he needs more tea.
She is, despite herself, already attending to him.
The social geometry of that scene is precise in a way we can underestimate.
Tea-making in this period was the hostess's sovereign domain — it was one of the very few performances of domestic authority that a gentlewoman exercised in public.
And here is Margaret, a clergyman's daughter from the south, performing that role for a northern manufacturer she considers socially her inferior.
The proud air of an unwilling slave is not mere character colour — it is the exact social transaction Gaskell wants us to feel.
She is obliged by courtesy to serve someone she has already decided she will not respect.
And then Gaskell gives us the contrast that undoes her — or begins to.
Margaret looks up from her work and sees the two men side by side — her father and Thornton — and the physical contrast strikes her like a kind of revelation.
Her father: soft lines, arched lids, an almost feminine languor.
And then this description of Thornton — listen to what Gaskell does with it.
The straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set, earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking at.
Without being unpleasantly sharp — that qualification is doing everything.
She is reassuring herself, even as she is arrested by him.
And that smile — Gaskell's description of Thornton's rare smile is one of the finest physical portraits in the book.
The lines in the face were few but firm, as if they were carved in marble — and then that sudden sunlight when the smile comes.
What moves me is that Margaret, at this early stage, already likes that smile — it is the first thing she has admired in him.
She is ahead of her own conscious mind — which is, of course, precisely how the deepest attachments form.
Which makes the next move all the more mordantly funny.
Because we then cut to Thornton leaving — and what does he mutter to himself?
'A more proud, disagreeable girl I never saw. Even her great beauty is blotted out of one's memory by her scornful ways.'
Even her great beauty is blotted out — which is to say, he has been cataloguing her great beauty in considerable detail throughout the entire visit.
The self-deception is so transparent that it practically winks at the reader.
He's furious with her — and furious with himself for noticing her.
And she has handed him his tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave and not given him a second thought.
This is the asymmetry at the heart of everything that follows — and Gaskell plants it here, in a bracelet and a teacup, with no fuss at all.
A bracelet and a teacup, and an empire of feeling beneath them.
Edmund, James, Caroline — this has been a conversation I could continue for another hour.
North and South rewards exactly this kind of attention — the more closely you read, the more it gives back.
Thank you to our listeners for joining us for North and South Unpacked — and to our three remarkable guests for bringing their knowledge, their disagreements, and their evident love of this novel.
Until next time.

c11:p12.text:
Margaret had noticed her mother’s jaded appearance with anxiety for some
time past, and this remark of her father’s sent her up to bed with a dim
fear lying like a weight on her heart. The life in Milton was so
different from what Mrs. Hale had been accustomed to live in Helstone,
in and out perpetually into the fresh and open air; the air itself was
so different, deprived of all revivifying principle as it seemed to be
here; the domestic worries pressed so very closely, and in so new and
sordid a form, upon all the women in the family, that there was good
reason to fear that her mother’s health might be becoming seriously
affected. There were several other signs of something wrong about Mrs.
Hale. She and Dixon held mysterious consultations in her bedroom, from
which Dixon would come out crying and cross, as was her custom when any
distress of her mistress called upon her sympathy. Once Margaret had
gone into the chamber soon after Dixon left it, and found her mother on
her knees, and as Margaret stole out she caught a few words which were
evidently a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily
suffering. Margaret yearned to re-unite the bond of intimate confidence
which had been broken by her long residence at her aunt Shaw’s, and
strove by gentle caresses and softened words to creep into the warmest
place in her mother’s heart. But though she received caresses and fond
words back again, in such profusion as would have gladdened her
formerly, yet she felt that there was a secret withheld from her, and
she believed it bore serious reference to her mother’s health. She lay
awake very long this night, planning how to lessen the evil influence of
their Milton life on her mother. A servant to give Dixon permanent
assistance should be got, if she gave up her whole time to the search;
and then, at any rate, her mother might have all the personal attention
she required, and had been accustomed to her whole life.
c11:p12.summary: Margaret observes signs of her mother's declining health and hidden suffering, contrasting Milton's harsh air and sordid domestic cares with her former life at Helstone, and resolves to ease her mother's burden.

“Oh, papa! you don’t mean that you thought me so silly? I really liked
that account of himself better than anything else he said. Everything
else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so
simply—with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of
shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother, that I was
less likely to leave the room then than when he was boasting about
Milton, as if there was not such another place in the world; or quietly
professing to despise people for careless, wasteful improvidence,
without ever seeming to think it his duty to try to make them
different,—to give them anything of the training which his mother gave
him, and to which he evidently owes his position, whatever that may be.
No! his statement of having been a shop-boy was the thing I liked best
of all.”

“You are mistaken,” said Margaret, roused by the aspersion on her
beloved South to a fond vehemence of defence, that brought the colour
into her cheeks and the angry tears into her eyes. “You do not know
anything about the South. If there is less adventure or less progress—I
suppose I must not say less excitement—from the gambling spirit of
trade, which seems requisite to force out these wonderful inventions,
there is less suffering also. I see men here going about in the streets
who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only
sufferers but haters. Now, in the South we have our poor, but there is
not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of
injustice which I see here. You do not know the South, Mr. Thornton,”
she concluded, collapsing into a determined silence, and angry with
herself for having said so much.

“Don’t fear!” said his mother, crushing down her own personal
mortification at the little notice he had taken of the rare ebullition
of her maternal feelings—of the pang of jealousy that betrayed the
intensity of her disregarded love. “Don’t be afraid,” she said, coldly.
“As far as love may go she may be worthy of you. It must have taken a
good deal to overcome her pride. Don’t be afraid, John,” said she,
kissing him, as she wished him good-night. And she went slowly and
majestically out of the room. But when she got into her own, she locked
the door, and sate down to cry unwonted tears.

And she swept out of it with the noiseless grace of an offended
princess. Mrs. Thornton had quite enough of natural humour to make her
feel the ludricrousness of the position in which she was left. There was
nothing for it but to show herself out. She was not particularly annoyed
at Margaret’s way of behaving. She did not care enough for her for that.
She had taken Mrs. Thornton’s remonstrance to the full as keenly to
heart as that lady expected; and Margaret’s passion at once mollified
her visitor, far more than any silence or reserve could have done. It
showed the effect of her words. “My young lady,” thought Mrs. Thornton
to herself; “you’ve a pretty good temper of your own. If John and you
had come together, he would have had to keep a tight hand over you, to
make you know your place. But I don’t think you will go a-walking again
with your beau, at such an hour of the day, in a hurry. You’ve too much
pride and spirit in you for that. I like to see a girl fly out at the
notion of being talked about. It shows they’re neither giddy, nor bold
by nature. As for that girl, she might be bold, but she’d never be
giddy. I’ll do her that justice. Now as to Fanny, she’d be giddy, and
not bold. She’s no courage in her, poor thing!”

“Well, sir,” said Higgins, rather doggedly; “it might, or it might not.
There’s two opinions go to settling that point. But suppose it was truth
double strong, it were no truth to me if I couldna take it in. I daresay
there’s great truth in yon Latin book on your shelves; but it’s
gibberish and not truth to me, unless I know the meaning o’ the words.
If yo’, sir, or any other knowledgable, patient man comes to me, and
